NOVELTY STATEMENT
The standard practice delivers a maintenance intervention based on scheduled coolant heater checks and starter motor replacement, which is a CONFIGURATION/MODIFICATION approach. My mechanism departs by using a CONFIGURATION of existing telemetry (a diagnostic algorithm) to predict the failure without altering the physical system, utilizing a DIRECT TRANSFER of flow/pressure logic to current/voltage signatures. The failure-physics connection is that cold-start failure in standby gensets is primarily driven by the interaction of low coolant temperature reducing cranking torque requirements (changing the load curve) and battery voltage sag under load; when the starter battery cannot maintain sufficient voltage to drive the motor past the compression resistance at low temp, the engine will not reach flameout speed.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is the electrical power balance and motor torque-speed characteristic. \( P = V_{battery} \times I_{crank} \). As temperature drops, the internal resistance of the battery increases (approx. \( R_{int} \) rises with \( T^{-1} \) in Arrhenius terms for electrolyte conductivity), and the engine's compression resistance \( N(\omega) \) increases relative to ambient because oil viscosity increases and air density is higher. The critical failure threshold is when \( V_{terminal} < V_{min} \) required to sustain \( \omega > \omega_{flameout} \).
Magnitude verification: A 2 MVA genset typically uses a 12V or 24V starter. Assume 24V system. Cranking current \( I_{crank} \) is typically 300-600A. Voltage drop across internal resistance \( R_{int} \) is \( V_{drop} = I \times R_{int} \). If \( R_{int} \) rises from 5m\(\Omega\) (healthy, warm) to 15m\(\Omega\) (aged/cold), \( V_{drop} \) goes from 1.5V to 4.5V. Terminal voltage drops from 22.5V to 19.5V. The motor torque \( \tau = k \phi I \) drops as \( V_{terminal} \) drops. If the load torque required to turn over the engine at -10C exceeds the torque available at 19.5V, stall occurs. This is verifiable via the recorded telemetry.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
(a) Algorithm module: Deploy a diagnostic rule-based engine into the existing PLC/SCADA HMI. Inputs: Cranking Current (ALREADY-RECORDED via existing starter wire telemetry), Coolant Temperature (ALREADY-RECORDED via jacket water heater/thermistor telemetry), Starter Battery Voltage (ALREADY-RECORDED via existing bus voltage sensor). Reference Thresholds: \( V_{min\_flameout} \) DERIVED from stated motor nameplate specifications (torque vs. voltage curve) and the known minimum flameout speed (e.g., 40-50 RPM for a medium-speed diesel). The threshold is calculated by solving for the minimum terminal voltage that produces sufficient torque to overcome the peak compression resistance at the lowest recorded coolant temperature. No new hardware is procured.
BURDEN LEDGER
(a) Installability: The algorithm is software-only; it is installed on the existing control system. Burden is SAME as standard practice's "check heater" procedure, as it requires no new cables, sensors, or wiring.
(b) Operability: The system automatically logs the "Cold Start Health Index" (CSI) for every start event. It flags "High Risk" if the calculated terminal voltage sag exceeds the derived threshold. This is lighter than the standard practice's manual inspection of heater elements, as it requires zero physical intervention.
(c) Maintenance: Zero additional maintenance. The algorithm self-validates against the known physics of the battery/motor pair. Cost class is identical to the standard practice's monitoring (which is often absent or manual), but provides a predictive capability.

EXECUTABLE TEST
(a) Protocol: Retrieve the last 12 months of logged cranking current profiles, coolant temperature readings, and battery voltage traces from the existing SCADA/Historian.
(b) Pass/Fail Threshold: For each historical start event, calculate the "Peak Voltage Sag" (\( V_{open} - V_{min\_during\_crank} \)). Correlate this sag with the recorded coolant temperature. Define a pass condition: The model correctly predicts "Start Success" if \( V_{terminal\_calculated} > V_{min\_flameout} \) and "Start Failure" if \( V_{terminal\_calculated} \le V_{min\_flameout} \).
(c) Kill Criterion: If the model cannot achieve >95% predictive accuracy on historical data (or if the physical relationship between voltage sag and start failure is not linear/predictable due to other hidden factors like fuel injection timing), the method is invalidated. The test validates the mechanism against ALREADY-RECORDED data.

CONSTRAINT BIND
The primary stated indicator is the **Starter Battery Voltage** (specifically, the dynamic sag during cranking). The cranking current and coolant temperature are secondary indicators used to contextualize the load and thermal state. The predictor must focus on the voltage sag because that is the direct electrical manifestation of the battery's inability to deliver power, which is the root cause of the no-start event in a standby genset with a functioning fuel system. The question explicitly states "use only... starter battery voltage telemetry" as a key input, and the failure mode "cold-start-failure" is directly linked to battery performance degradation in low thermal mass environments.
